item.title: Yap state officials send team to assist Yapese on Guam with voter services
item.description: The Yap State Election Office and the Office of the Attorney General of Yap have sent a team to provide voter assistance for Yapese people living on Guam who need to vote in Yap State. New voter registration is offered for students studying in Guam. These voters must bring a valid passport or birth certificate and an enrollment letter from their institution.
item.content:encoded:
The Yap State Election Office and the Office of the Attorney General of Yap have sent a team to provide voter assistance for Yapese people living on Guam who need to vote in Yap State.

New voter registration is offered for students studying in Guam. These voters must bring a valid passport or birth certificate and an enrollment letter from their institution.

Reregistration is offered for voters with name changes that do not match the election master list.

Assistance will also be provided for voters needing help with absentee ballot requests.

The voter assistance initiative began Tuesday and continued Wedneday. The final day is Friday, with a session from 10 a.m. to noon, and another from 2 to 4 p.m. at the Yapese Community Centre in Chalan Pago.

All participants are required to bring their FSM passport and any other necessary documents in order to be assisted.

item.title: WASC restores accreditation for Guam schools after purchase order problem resolved
item.description: The Western Association of Schools and Colleges has restored full accreditation for Guam schools, following an announcement earlier this week that accreditation had been terminated. Guam Department of Education spokesperson Damen Michael Borja said that termination stemmed from an outstanding purchase order payment from the 2024-25 school year.
item.content:encoded:
The Western Association of Schools and Colleges has restored full accreditation for Guam schools, following an announcement earlier this week that accreditation had been terminated.

Guam Department of Education spokesperson Damen Michael Borja said that termination stemmed from an outstanding purchase order payment from the 2024-25 school year.

GDOE officials worked with WASC and took care of the payment on Monday.

"We inherited this issue, and we took it on directly by reviewing the invoices, correcting the billing errors, and staying in constant communication with WASC,” Superintendent Judith Won Pat stated in a news release. “I'm grateful for their confirmation that our accreditation is continuous, and our focus remains on making sure our schools and students are never adversely affected."

In written confirmation to the department, WASC stated that there was no break in membership in good standing and that accreditation is considered continuous.

All GDOE schools remain accredited through school year 2029.

item.title: Police, AG investigating death of murder suspect Nicholas Wayne Moore
item.description: The Guam Police Department and the Office of the Attorney General are asking for information from the public as they investigate the death of murder suspect Nicholas Wayne Moore. Moore’s attorney, Mike Phillips, issued a statement Wednesday.
item.content:encoded:
The Guam Police Department and the Office of the Attorney General are asking for information from the public as they investigate the death of murder suspect Nicholas Wayne Moore.

Moore’s attorney, Mike Phillips, issued a statement Wednesday.

“Nicholas was found early this morning in his bedroom. It was clear at that time Nicholas passed away. At this time his passing is being investigated and the cause of death remains unknown,” Phillips said.

He said the family is working with investigators.

Moore was charged in the 2020 killing of Michael Jose Castro, whose car was found in the compound of Unitek Environmental, a company run by Moore’s father.

Moore was also charged in a separate 2020 Agana Heights shooting that sent a man to the hospital. After numerous delays, a mistrial was declared in that case in 2023.

He had also been indicted in a criminal sexual conduct case involving a girl under the age of 16.

“We are shocked by Nicholas’ passing and just met with him yesterday,” Phillips said. “We mourn Nicholas’ passing and look forward to receiving information regarding the cause of death.”

On Wednesday, police and Attorney General Douglas Moylan issued a statement saying they were investigating the circumstances surrounding the death.

“Because this remains an active investigation, authorities are limiting the release of additional information at this time to protect the integrity of the investigation,” the statement said. “We specifically ask that anyone who has information as to the circumstances leading up to Mr. Nicholas Moore’s untimely death please come forward to speak with a GPD Criminal Investigation Division detective.”

Police can be reached at (671) 475-8615/6/7, or tips can be anonymously submitted online with Guam Crime Stoppers at www.guamcrimestoppers.com .

item.title: What is the pneumonic plague?
item.description: The ancient word "plague" is back in the headlines. NPR's Russia correspondent Charles Maynes reported this week on what we know about a Russian researcher working in a lab studying the plague who died from pneumonia of an unknown origin last week.
item.content:encoded:
The ancient word "plague" is back in the headlines.

NPR's Russia correspondent Charles Maynes reported this week on what we know about a Russian researcher working in a lab studying the plague who died from pneumonia of an unknown origin last week.

Maynes reports that the employee was a 28-year-old woman who worked in a lab in Siberia, some 2,500 miles from Moscow. An investigation by Russia's consumer health watchdog concluded that no pathogens in her body were connected to her work with infectious disease.

But local media have raised concerns about the spread of pneumonic plague, which NPR has not independently confirmed.

It's one of the diseases studied at the lab in Siberia. It's airborne and can be fatal.

While noting that 200 "contacts" were in quarantine, Russia has denied that there are cases of plague in the area. But questions loom. In a press conference Wednesday, the head of the World Health Organization, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said these Russian assurances were — at the very least — incomplete: "We don't yet have the full picture of this event and we're not able to conduct a full risk assessment. "

In the meantime, here's what we do know about the bacterial disease of plague — and the variant known as pneumonic plague.

The plague comes in several versions, depending on which body part the bacteria invade. When a flea bites a person, the individual typically develops what's called bubonic plague. In this case, the telltale sign is one or more swollen and painful lymph nodes, known as buboes. (The word "bubonic" comes from the Greek boubon , which means groin, because some people have swollen lymph nodes in their groin.) Doctors can diagnose the disease by taking a sample from the person's blood or lymph nodes and then submitting the sample to a lab for testing.

But when the bacteria spread to the lungs, this can cause what's called pneumonic plague. In this case, there's often no telltale sign of the plague, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

This version is much more dangerous, says medical entomologist Adelaide Miarinjara at Emory University. "It transmits pretty easily between people because it spreads through droplets, almost like COVID spreads."

And people can die more quickly with pneumonic plague than other forms, she adds, because the disease progresses more rapidly. "The key here is early diagnosis. If people aren't expecting it or don't seek treatment, they can die."

Treatment involves antibiotics, often administered by IV infusion.

In 2017, Madagascar suffered a large outbreak of pneumonic plague when a person from a rural part of the country brought the disease to the coastal city of Toamasina. That city hadn't seen a case of the plague in nearly a century, says Miarinjara, who was in Madagascar at the time. "A person transmitted the disease on public transportation," she says.

The country recorded more than 2,400 suspected cases, including nearly 1,900 cases of pneumonic plague. One study estimated that about 25% of people with confirmed cases died in this outbreak.

As for the reports of Russian "contacts" of the lab worker under quarantine — that reflects a long-standing response to sicknesses like the plague.

The idea of isolating, or quarantining, sick people dates back at least 3,000 years. The Book of Leviticus in the Bible mentions how to isolate people with leprosy.

The word "quarantine" itself arose during the Black Death, when the city-state of Dubrovnik, now part of the country of Croatia, enacted what is likely the first state-imposed isolation.

At the time, Dubrovnik was a wealthy merchant city along the coast of the Adriatic Sea. City leaders wanted to keep the bubonic plague out. So they began to force visitors to wait for 40 days on a remote island outside the city before coming ashore.

They called the wait quarantino , from the Italian word for "40."

"The first quarantine was pretty much improvised," Ivana Marinavić, the head of educational programs at the Lazarettos of Dubrovnik , told NPR in 2021 . The Lazarettos were the first buildings ever constructed for the sole purpose of quarantining.

If you broke the quarantine during the plague, the consequences were severe. "Torture, or cutting your nose or your ears off," Marinavić told NPR.

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

item.title: A childhood bike crash led to a stranger's gift — and a hidden message
item.description: When Rika Matsuda was 7, she got a new bike. "And I went to the park and started to ride it," Matsuda said, recalling the moment 10 years later, at 17. She told her story to an interpreter in her native Japanese.
item.content:encoded:
When Rika Matsuda was 7, she got a new bike.

"And I went to the park and started to ride it," Matsuda said, recalling the moment 10 years later, at 17. She told her story to an interpreter in her native Japanese.

"At first I was really excited because the bike was really, really fast."

But when she tried the brakes, nothing happened, and she slammed into a wall.

"My foot started to hurt and turned purple," Matsuda said. "It hurt so much that I had to sit down."

A few minutes later, she saw a man in his 20s walking toward her. She remembers him as large and muscular and wearing a suit. He was a stranger, and she was only 7, so she wasn't sure if she could trust him.

"But when he said, 'Are you OK?' I knew from his kind and gentle voice that he was a very nice man," Matsuda recalled.

The man took her to a water fountain and helped her wash her injured foot. Then he gave Matsuda his phone to call her grandfather. As they waited, the man pulled out a piece of paper from his bag and showed her how to fold an origami crane.

"He was really good at folding origami, and he taught me the right way to make a clean and beautiful crane," she said. "Maybe he wanted me to think about the paper instead of my foot."

When her grandfather arrived, the man helped get Matsuda and her bike back home.

"As we parted, he didn't say anything. He just smiled and handed me the origami crane," she said.

Later, she put the crane in her desk. Every so often, she would see it and remember the man's kindness.

Ten years later, as a high school student, Matsuda found herself thinking about that moment again. In English class, her teacher, Benjamin Johnson, introduced the students to My Unsung Hero and had them write stories of their own. She thought back to when she crashed her bike and the man who came to her rescue.

"I started to think deeply about that time and tried to remember the details," she said. "And I thought that maybe while I was on the phone with my grandfather, possibly [the man] wrote something on the paper."

She hurried home from school and unfolded the crane to check. He had. Inside was a well-known Japanese expression about how every encounter is precious.

Roughly, it means "We should treasure each time we cross paths with someone because it might never happen again." Or, more simply, "cherish the moment."

"Then I realized even more how kind and how nice of a man he was," Matsuda said. " And I thought, he's really my unsung hero."

item.title: This surprising mammal fossil is giving scientists something to chew on
item.description: Over the years, a section of the Inner Mongolia region of China has coughed up heaps of remarkable fossils, ranging from feathered dinosaurs to flying reptiles. "To say it's [a] hot spot is actually [an] understatement," says Zhe-Xi Luo , a paleontologist at the University of Chicago.
item.content:encoded:
Over the years, a section of the Inner Mongolia region of China has coughed up heaps of remarkable fossils, ranging from feathered dinosaurs to flying reptiles.

"To say it's [a] hot spot is actually [an] understatement," says Zhe-Xi Luo , a paleontologist at the University of Chicago.

Many of these fossils wind up at the nearby Paleontological Museum of Liaoning, a facility that Luo and his colleague, Thomas Martin of the University of Bonn, visit each year to examine new finds. A decade ago, a specimen in a thick slab of shale caught their eye.

It was the fossilized bones and soft tissue impressions of an ancient mammal that lived some 165 million years ago. "Early fossil mammals — in fact, they are exceedingly rare," says Luo.

This animal, which the team named Megacauda sungei and have described in the journal Nature , was a prize discovery. The remains were so intact that it was possible to determine that it was likely capable of chewing food and then swallowing it, and also suckling — traits that are shared by mammals.

Luo and his colleagues conclude that these evolutionary innovations — and their presence among our ancient mammalian relatives — extend deep into the past to at least the middle Jurassic.

"It's all there in one remarkable fossil," says Luo.

The fossil was about the size of a chihuahua, but somewhat hard to discern from the rock surrounding it.

"The fossil itself is actually very dark," explains Luo. "The bones are black, the slab [is] dark. And it's kind of difficult to have beautiful photographs."

One of his collaborators, Chang-Fu Zhou of Shandong University of Science and Technology, snapped a different kind of vivid image using a technique called X-ray fluorescence spectroscopy. "It would make this bone pop out in different colors," says Luo.

The resulting image rendered the skeleton a bright yellow and it showcased a curious combination of characteristics. The back end, which includes the pelvis, hind limbs, and tail, resembles a modern-day platypus.

These features suggest that this animal was likely semi-aquatic and foraged in the water. "The big tail is good for swimming," says Luo.

"However," he continues, "its teeth and the jaw would be very different from platypus. So the head is very much of a predator." Indeed, Luo and his colleagues found a smattering of small salamander bones inside the fossil that they suspect the animal had eaten by first cutting and shearing with its sharp teeth.

There was something else that Luo instantly noticed about the fossil. "My eyes zeroed in on these tiny hyoid bones," he recalls.

The human hyoid bone sits in the throat, half an inch or so above the Adam's apple, and supports the backside of the tongue.

The team later CT scanned the fossil, including the underside of the skull, which exposed a delicate roof of the mouth as well as a series of bone hooks and ridges.

With this combination of rarely preserved features, "we are able with great confidence to reconstruct the whole muscular skeletal machinery," says Luo.

This reconstruction revealed that the animal was likely capable of doing two things that are unique to mammals.

The first is swallowing food after chewing it. Other vertebrates tend to bite and gulp. But mammals "chew down all the food with our teeth," Luo says. "And then we swallow one bolus of food down to our esophagus at a time."

Consider, for a moment, a carnivore that chews meat, an herbivore that crunches on vegetables, and an insect-eater that chomps bugs. This diverse array of foods all get chewed up and then swallowed down a mammalian throat in a similar way.

Secondly, this fossil appears to have been capable of suckling, which embodies something even more fundamental.

"That ability to suckle mother's milk literally defined our biology," says Luo. "And that's why our group is called mammals. We're named after the mammary glands."

This is some of the oldest fossil evidence of an animal with both these key mammalian abilities.

"It's a fascinating specimen," says Jessica Theodor , a paleontologist at the University of Calgary who wasn't involved in the research. "The whole setup looks more like what we see in modern mammals."

Theodor would like to see some of the images in greater detail, but she says a fossil like this tracks the evolution of lactation, which she likens to a kind of dietary and hormonal conversation between mother and baby.

"The conversation is beginning very far back in the Mesozoic — in the Jurassic and Cretaceous," says Theodor. "That's amazing to me that it's this old and this fundamental."

For Luo, this fossil is the latest evidence of how new ways of feeding have helped mammals and their predecessors diversify — even back when they were the little guys on the proverbial block.

"Mammals, they're never dominant in the age of dinosaurs," he says. "But nonetheless, they hold out relatively well compared to all other vertebrates."

By the time of the Jurassic period, there were already proto-mammalian gliders, swimmers, land-dwellers, tree-dwellers and diggers. Each one was making a living in its own distinct way — all united in their shared ability to chew, swallow and suckle.

item.title: Judge orders that Christa Pike execution evidence be preserved
item.description: The Davidson County Chancery Court in Nashville ordered Tennessee prison officials to preserve all evidence in connection with last week's botched lethal injection of Christa Pike, including log books, medical waste and all messages sent or received by officials associated with the execution attempt. "Anything in the actual room needs to be preserved and maintained," Judge I'Ashea Myles said.
item.content:encoded:
The Davidson County Chancery Court in Nashville ordered Tennessee prison officials to preserve all evidence in connection with last week's botched lethal injection of Christa Pike, including log books, medical waste and all messages sent or received by officials associated with the execution attempt.

"Anything in the actual room needs to be preserved and maintained," Judge I'Ashea Myles said.

The judge also granted a request from Pike's attorneys for "liberal access" to their client, ordering that prison officials will have two hours to respond to requests from lawyers for in-person visits with Pike.

Speaking outside the courtroom, Luke P. Ihnen, an assistant federal defender in Knoxville, told reporters that this was "just a first step of many to preserve and enforce Christa's constitutional rights after this unprecedented botched execution."

The hearing came a week after Pike was left hospitalized and in critical condition following the Sept. 30 execution attempt in which she was strapped to a gurney and administered two doses of pentobarbital, a barbiturate widely used in U.S. executions. But several minutes after the first dose, she said her arm was burning and asked whether it was supposed to feel that way. She then said, "Please try up on my shoulder higher."

Pike's attorneys said that after days of unconsciousness, Pike was awake again, speaking and continuing to receive critical medical care.

Randy Spivey, a post-conviction attorney representing Pike, called his client "a survivor."

"She survived sexual abuse [and] the rapes of multiple men. She survived a suicide attempt when she was 12 and she survived the state's attempt to execute her," he said. "She deserves answers about what was done to her and the people of Tennessee deserve those answers, too."

He said of the botched execution, "all of this was foreseen," because Pike has a medical condition that would make it difficult to insert an IV to deliver the lethal doses of pentobarbital.

Spivey, who was a witness to last week's failed execution, told NPR that after a second dose, Pike fell unconscious but continued breathing and making sounds like choking. It "went on for so long," he said.

Following the failed execution, Tennessee's top prison official, Frank Strada, resigned, and the state's governor, Bill Lee, halted executions through the end of the year and ordered an independent investigation into the state's capital punishment system.

It wasn't immediately clear whether that would affect a second attempt to execute Pike, but speaking at Wednesday's hearing, Tennessee Assistant Attorney General John Ayers said the decision on when or if to schedule a new execution date was up to the state's supreme court.

Ihnen, one of the defense attorneys, said it would be "unconscionable that the state would try to execute her again."

Pike was on death row for a murder she committed at age 18. In 1995, she and her boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, tortured and killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a fellow classmate in the Knoxville Job Corps. Shipp, who was a minor at the time of the crime, received life in prison without parole for his part in the murder.

In a clemency petition filed last month, Pike's attorneys asked that her sentence be commuted to life in prison without the possibility of parole, citing her history of childhood trauma.

"Local and national media covered Christa's trial in the midst of the 'Satanic Panic' of the 1990s," the attorneys said. "In truth, it was Christa's abusive boyfriend and co-defendant, Tadaryl Shipp, who was fascinated by satanic imagery."

The media at the time had "focused on the salacious parts of Christa's crime, disregarding the context of her youth, trauma, and mental illness," they added.

Critics of the death penalty are outraged at what happened to Pike during the attempt to execute her.

"This failed attempt is the worst we've ever seen and unlike any other botched execution in the modern era," Robin M. Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said in a statement .

The Death Penalty Information Center, a nonpartisan, nonprofit organization, said Pike was the first person in the history of capital punishment to survive after being injected with lethal drugs.
